goal: After this you can read the three sizes of a 3-D array, say how many elements it holds, initialise it, and visit every element with three nested loops.
warmup: Your university keeps the marks of students for two terms. For one term you can draw a table: one row per student, one column per subject. That is a 2-D table. Now put the second term's table behind the first one, like pages in a notebook. To find one mark you need three things: which term (page), which student (row), which subject (column). A 3-D array is exactly a stack of such tables.
definition: A 3-D array is an array whose every element is a 2-D array. It is declared with three sizes: type name[layers][rows][columns];. For example int a[2][3][4]; has 2 layers, each layer has 3 rows, and each row has 4 columns. The total number of elements is the product of the three sizes: 2 x 3 x 4 = 24. An element is reached with three indexes in the same order: a[layer][row][column]. Every index starts from 0.
howItWorks: There is no 3-D model to look at in memory. Think of the layers as pages: the first index chooses the page, the second index chooses the row on that page, and the third chooses the column. The computer actually stores all elements in one long line, layer after layer, row after row (see the flattened array visual). For initialisation use nested braces: one pair for the whole array, one pair for each layer, one pair for each row. To visit every element use three nested loops, one for each index. The outer loop is the layer, the middle loop is the row, the inner loop is the column. The loop limits must be the three sizes in the same order as the declaration, and each loop uses < (never <=), because the last valid index is size - 1. Total elements = layers x rows x columns, so int a[2][3][4] holds 24 values and the innermost statement runs 24 times.

worked.problem: The marks of 3 students in 3 subjects are stored for 2 terms in int marks[2][3][3]. Print the table of each term, then add up all the marks of student 1 over both terms.
pseudocode: SET marks (2 terms x 3 students x 3 subjects)
FOR each term t: PRINT the heading
FOR each student s: FOR each subject j: PRINT marks[t][s][j]
FOR each term t: FOR each subject j: total = total + marks[t][1][j]
PRINT number of elements and total

  E --> C
  C -->|No| F[total = 0]
  F --> G["Add marks t 1 j for all t and j"]
  G --> H[/Print elements and total/]

worked.problem: Write a program that reads the 8 values of a 2 x 2 x 2 array from the keyboard and prints the largest value with its three indexes.
pseudocode: READ the 8 values into a[l][r][c] with three loops
SET big = a[0][0][0] and its place (0, 0, 0)
FOR l, r, c over all elements:
IF a[l][r][c] > big THEN big = a[l][r][c], save l, r, c
PRINT big and the three indexes

  C --> D{More elements?}
  D -->|Yes| E{"element > big?"}
  E -->|Yes| F[Save big and l, r, c]
  E -->|No| D
  F --> D
  D -->|No| G[/Print big and its place/]
  G --> H([End])

int a[3][4][5]  ->  3 layers, 4 rows, 5 columns, 3 x 4 x 5 = 60 elements

mistakes.wrong:
int a[2][3][4];
a[2][0][0] = 5;   // layers are 0 and 1 only
mistakes.right:
int a[2][3][4];
a[1][0][0] = 5;   // last valid layer is size - 1
mistakes.error: No compiler error. Index 2 is outside an array with 2 layers, so the program writes into memory that does not belong to the array. This can crash or give wrong results.
No compiler error. The loop limits do not follow the declaration order, so the program reads beyond the array and prints garbage.
No compiler error. With only two indexes the result is a whole row, not a number, so you do not see the value you wanted. A 3-D array needs three indexes to reach one element.

examTips: Read the declaration slowly: the first size is the number of layers, the second is rows, the third is columns. Write 'layers x rows x columns' next to it.
Total elements = product of all three sizes. int a[3][4][5] has 60 elements.
A 3-D array needs three nested loops, and the limits must match the sizes in the same order. The innermost statement runs total-elements times.
Valid indexes run from 0 to size - 1. Say it in your answer when you explain an out-of-range error.
In real-life questions, decide what each index means first: for example marks[term][student][subject].
romanSummary: 3-D array bohat si 2-D tables ka set hai, jaise kitaab ke pages: int a[layers][rows][cols].
Total elements teeno sizes ko multiply karne se milte hain. Misal: a[2][3][4] mein 2 x 3 x 4 = 24 elements hain.
Ek element tak pahunchne ke liye teen index lagte hain: a[layer][row][column], aur index 0 se shuru hota hai.
Poore array ko process karne ke liye teen nested loops lagte hain: bahar layer ka loop, beech mein row ka, andar column ka.
